nodes.summary: The kind of access an operation makes to its data item is one of two values: a read or a write.
nodes.title: Read or write access

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule in which no operation occurs twice, and let $L$ be a topological order of the precedence graph of $s$. Then the schedule obtained from $s$ by stably sorting its operations by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is conflict-equivalent to $s$.
nodes.title: Serializing along a topological order preserves conflict equivalence

nodes.summary: A schedule $s'$ is conflict-equivalent to a schedule $s$ when $s'$ is a permutation of $s$ and, for any two operations $a$ and $b$ that belong to the same transaction or conflict, an occurrence of $a$ comes before an occurrence of $b$ in $s$ if and only if the same holds in $s'$.
nodes.title: Conflict equivalence

nodes.summary: A schedule without duplicate operations is conflict-serializable exactly when its precedence graph is acyclic.
nodes.title: The serializability theorem

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule in which no operation occurs twice. If $r$ is a function from the transactions to the natural numbers with $r(i) < r(j)$ whenever the precedence graph of $s$ has an edge from $i$ to $j$, then $s$ is conflict-serializable.
nodes.title: A rank increasing along precedence edges gives conflict serializability

nodes.summary: A schedule $s$ is conflict-serializable when some serial schedule is conflict-equivalent to $s$.
nodes.title: Conflict-serializable schedule

nodes.summary: Two operations of a schedule conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of the two accesses is a write.
nodes.title: Conflicting operations

nodes.summary: If a schedule $s$ in which no operation occurs twice is conflict-serializable, then the precedence graph of $s$ is acyclic.
nodes.title: A conflict-serializable schedule has an acyclic precedence graph

nodes.summary: Let $s$ be a schedule and $L$ a list in which every transaction occurs. Then the schedule obtained from $s$ by stably sorting its operations by the first position of their transaction in $L$ is serial.
nodes.title: Serializing along a complete transaction order gives a serial schedule

nodes.summary: A schedule $s$ is serial when, for any two distinct transactions $i$ and $j$, either every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $j$ in $s$, or every operation of $j$ in $s$ occurs before every operation of $i$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Serial schedule

nodes.summary: For $n$ transactions, numbered $0, \dots, n - 1$, and data items of type $X$, an operation consists of a transaction $t \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, an occurrence identifier $k \in \mathbb{N}$, an access, which is a read or a write, and a data item $x \in X$: transaction $t$ reads or writes $x$, and $k$ makes repeated accesses of $t$ to an item distinct operations.
nodes.title: Operation of a schedule

nodes.summary: Two operations $a$ and $b$ are order-relevant when they belong to the same transaction or they conflict. These are the pairs whose relative order a conflict-equivalent schedule must keep.
nodes.title: Operations whose relative order matters

nodes.summary: For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and $j$, there is a precedence edge from $i$ to $j$ in $s$ when some operation of $i$ occurs in $s$ before some operation of $j$ in $s$ that conflicts with it.
nodes.title: Edge of the precedence graph

nodes.summary: The precedence (serialization) graph of a schedule $s$ of $n$ transactions is the directed adjacency graph whose vertices are the transactions $0, \dots, n - 1$, listed in increasing order, and whose adjacency list at a transaction $i$ lists, in increasing order, the transactions $j$ such that there is a precedence edge from $i$ to $j$ in $s$.
nodes.title: Precedence graph

nodes.summary: For a list $\sigma$ of transactions and a schedule $s$, the serialization of $s$ along $\sigma$ sorts the operations of $s$ by the position of the first occurrence of their transaction in $\sigma$, where a transaction that does not occur in $\sigma$ gets the length of $\sigma$ as its position. The sort is stable: operations with the same position keep their relative order in $s$.
nodes.title: Serialization of a schedule along a transaction order

nodes.summary: For a schedule $s$ and transactions $i$ and $j$, transaction $i$ precedes transaction $j$ in $s$ when every operation of $i$ in $s$ occurs in $s$ before every operation of $j$ in $s$.
nodes.title: One transaction before another in a schedule

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
